claim: Debates have arisen as to whether non-human animals actually can learn abstract non-symbolic numerousness or whether they always rely on some continuous physical aspect of the stimuli, covarying with number.
source: Debates have arisen as to whether non-human animals actually can learn abstract non-symbolic numerousness or whether they always rely on some continuous physical aspect of the stimuli, covarying with number.
evidence: This is a statement about existing scientific debates, supported by the broader literature context.

claim: Archerfish were trained to select one of two groups of black dots in Experiment 1 with 3 vs 6 elements.
source: Archerfish were trained to select one of two groups of black dots (Exp. 1: 3 vs 6 elements; Exp. 2: 2 vs 3 elements)
evidence: This describes the experimental design and training conditions used in the study.

claim: Archerfish were trained to select one of two groups of black dots in Experiment 2 with 2 vs 3 elements.
source: Archerfish were trained to select one of two groups of black dots (Exp. 1: 3 vs 6 elements; Exp. 2: 2 vs 3 elements)
evidence: This describes the experimental design and training conditions used in the study.

claim: The training stimuli were controlled for several combinations of physical variables including elements' size, overall area, overall perimeter, density, and sparsity.
source: these were controlled for several combinations of physical variables (elements' size, overall area, overall perimeter, density, and sparsity), ensuring that only numerical information was available.
evidence: This describes the methodological controls applied in the experimental design.

claim: Only numerical information was available to the archerfish during training.
source: these were controlled for several combinations of physical variables (elements' size, overall area, overall perimeter, density, and sparsity), ensuring that only numerical information was available.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental design and controls applied.

claim: Generalization tests in Experiment 1 included novel numerical comparisons of 2 vs 3, 5 vs 8, and 6 vs 9.
source: Generalization tests with novel numerical comparisons (2 vs 3, 5 vs 8, and 6 vs 9 in Exp. 1; 3 vs 4, 3 vs 6 in Exp. 2)
evidence: This describes the test conditions used in the study.

claim: Generalization tests in Experiment 2 included novel numerical comparisons of 3 vs 4 and 3 vs 6.
source: Generalization tests with novel numerical comparisons (2 vs 3, 5 vs 8, and 6 vs 9 in Exp. 1; 3 vs 4, 3 vs 6 in Exp. 2)
evidence: This describes the test conditions used in the study.

claim: Archerfish chose the largest or smallest numerical group according to the relative number that was rewarded at training.
source: revealed choice for the largest or smallest numerical group according to the relative number that was rewarded at training.
evidence: This is a finding from the generalization tests reported in the study.

claim: None of the continuous physical variables, including spatial frequency, were affecting archerfish performance.
source: None of the continuous physical variables, including spatial frequency, were affecting archerfish performance.
evidence: This is a conclusion from statistical analyses of the experimental data.

claim: Archerfish spontaneously use abstract relative numerical information for both small and large numbers when only numerical cues are available.
source: Results provide evidence that archerfish spontaneously use abstract relative numerical information for both small and large numbers when only numerical cues are available.
evidence: This is the main conclusion drawn from the experimental results.

claim: Non-symbolic numerical estimation is an important and well-studied cognitive ability that allows humans and other animals to interact successfully with their surroundings.
source: Non-symbolic numerical estimation is an important and well-studied cognitive ability that allows humans and other animals to interact successfully with their surroundings.
evidence: This is a general statement about the field supported by established scientific knowledge.

claim: The development of a 'sense of number' is associated with fundamental biological needs that allow animals to estimate companions, enemies, or food in different patches.
source: The development of a 'sense of number' is associated with fundamental biological needs that in many ecological contexts allow animals to estimate how many companions or enemies are around, or how much food is present in different patches – all important information to maximize fitness and reproductive success in the wild (Nieder, 2020).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Nieder, 2020.

claim: Extensive evidence supports the use of numerical information in non-human primates.
source: Extensive evidence supports the use of numerical information in non-human primates (e.g. Anderson et al., 2005; Beran et al., 2008; Beran and Beran, 2004; Cantlon and Brannon, 2007; Smith et al., 2003)
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to prior research.

claim: Numerical abilities have been demonstrated in mammals.
source: as well as in other mammals (e.g. Abramson et al., 2013; Benson-Amram et al., 2011; McComb et al., 1994; Perdue et al., 2012; Vonk and Beran, 2012; West and Young, 2002)
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to prior research.

claim: Numerical abilities have been demonstrated in birds.
source: in birds (e.g. Bogale et al., 2014; Ditz and Nieder, 2016; Garland et al., 2012; Pepperberg, 2006; Rugani et al., 2013; Scarf and Colombo, 2011)
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to prior research.

claim: Numerical abilities have been demonstrated in amphibians.
source: in amphibians (e.g. Krusche et al., 2010; Stancher et al., 2015)
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to prior research.

claim: Numerical abilities have been demonstrated in reptiles.
source: in reptiles (e.g. Gazzola et al., 2018; Miletto Petrazzini et al., 2018)
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to prior research.

claim: Numerical abilities have been demonstrated in fish.
source: in fish (e.g. Gómez-Laplaza et al., 2018; Potrich et al., 2019; Stancher et al., 2013)
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to prior research.

claim: Numerical abilities have been demonstrated in arthropods.
source: and in arthropods (e.g. Dacke and Srinivasan, 2008; Gross et al., 2009; Nelson and Jackson, 2012; Rodríguez et al., 2015)
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to prior research.

claim: Numerical discrimination seems to be supported by an 'Approximate Number System' (ANS).
source: Numerical discrimination seems to be supported by an 'Approximate Number System' (ANS, Butterworth, 1999; Nieder and Dehaene, 2009)
evidence: This is supported by citations to Butterworth, 1999 and Nieder and Dehaene, 2009.

claim: The ANS discriminative accuracy is ratio dependent in accordance with Weber's law.
source: which discriminative accuracy is ratio dependent in accordance with Weber's law (as the ratio between two numerosity increases, the discrimination gets more difficult).
evidence: This describes a known property of the ANS based on established scientific knowledge.

claim: An attentional working memory-based system called the 'Object Tracking System' (OTS) has been claimed to provide precise representation of small numbers (up to 3–4).
source: Besides the ANS, an attentional working memory-based system has been claimed for by some authors as providing precise representation of small numbers (up to 3–4), the so-called 'Object Tracking System' (OTS; Trick and Pylyshyn, 1994)
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Trick and Pylyshyn, 1994.

claim: The generality of the Object Tracking System for non-human animals is debated.
source: though its generality for non-human animals is debated (discussion in Vallortigara, 2017; Vallortigara, 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to discussions in Vallortigara, 2017 and 2014.

claim: Neuronal response selectivity for number has been found in the parietal and prefrontal cortex in humans.
source: Studies investigating the neural basis of number representation revealed selectivity of neuronal response in some areas of the brain, such as the parietal and prefrontal cortex in humans (Kutter et al., 2018; Piazza et al., 2004)
evidence: This is supported by citations to Kutter et al., 2018 and Piazza et al., 2004.

claim: Neuronal response selectivity for number has been found in the parietal and prefrontal cortex in monkeys.
source: and in monkeys (Nieder et al., 2002; Nieder and Merten, 2007)
evidence: This is supported by citations to Nieder et al., 2002 and Nieder and Merten, 2007.

claim: Neuronal response selectivity for number has been found in the nidopallium caudolaterale in crows.
source: the nidopallium caudolaterale in crows (Ditz and Nieder, 2016; Ditz and Nieder, 2015)
evidence: This is supported by citations to Ditz and Nieder, 2016 and 2015.

claim: Neuronal response selectivity for number has been found in the most caudal dorsal-central part of the pallium in zebrafish.
source: and the most caudal dorsal-central part of the pallium in zebrafish (Messina et al., 2020; Messina et al., 2021a)
evidence: This is supported by citations to Messina et al., 2020 and 2021a.

claim: Common selective pressures led to convergent evolution of numerical representation in different species.
source: suggesting that common selective pressures led to convergent evolution of numerical representation in different species (Nieder, 2021; Vallortigara, 2021).
evidence: This is an interpretation supported by citations to Nieder, 2021 and Vallortigara, 2021.

claim: Numerical information is intrinsically melded with other non-numerical properties of the stimulus, such as area, density, spatial frequency, or elements' arrangement.
source: However, one issue in all these experiments is that animals are dealing with sets of physical elements, and thus numerical information is intrinsically melted with other non-numerical properties of the stimulus, such as the area, the density, the spatial frequency, or the elements' arrangement (Leibovich et al., 2017).
evidence: This is a methodological issue in the field supported by a citation to Leibovich et al., 2017.

claim: Some debates have arisen concerning whether bees use abstract numerical information or rather rely on sensory properties of the stimulus for discrimination.
source: Recently, some debates have arisen concerning whether bees use abstract numerical information or rather rely on sensory properties of the stimulus for discrimination (Howard et al., 2018; MaBouDi et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Howard et al., 2018 and MaBouDi et al., 2021.

claim: A sophisticated script for automatic generation of visual stimuli allows proper randomization and control of continuous physical variables in number sense experiments.
source: Taking advantage of the fact that we recently developed a sophisticated script for the automatic generation of visual stimuli that can allow proper randomization and control of continuous physical variables in number sense experiments (Zanon et al., 2021)
evidence: This describes a methodological tool developed by the authors, supported by a citation to Zanon et al., 2021.

claim: Archerfish are well known for their particular hunting strategy of spitting at preys above the water surface with a precise jet of water.
source: These fish are well known for their particular hunting strategy, which consists of spitting at preys above the water surface with a precise jet of water thrown with the mouth.
evidence: This is established knowledge about archerfish behavior.

claim: The archerfish hunting repertoire makes it very easy to train them to hit targets using operant conditioning.
source: This attacking repertoire makes it very easy to train them to hit targets using operant conditioning (see e.g. Newport and Schuster, 2020).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Newport and Schuster, 2020.

claim: No studies in archerfish have explicitly investigated abstract numerical abilities prior to this study.
source: Still, to date, no studies in archerfish have explicitly investigated abstract numerical abilities.
evidence: This is a statement about the state of the literature at the time of the study.

claim: When archerfish make magnitude-related decisions, their choice is influenced by non-numerical variables that positively correlate with numerosity.
source: Leibovich-Raveh et al., 2021 showed that when archerfish make magnitude-related decisions, their choice is influenced by the non-numerical variables that positively correlate with numerosity
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Leibovich-Raveh et al., 2021.

claim: When exposed to two groups of dots differing in number and continuous physical information, archerfish spontaneously selected the group containing the larger non-numerical magnitudes and smaller numerosity.
source: for instance, when exposed to two groups of dots differing in number and continuous physical information, archerfish spontaneously selected the group containing the larger non-numerical magnitudes and smaller numerosity, switching to the larger numerical set when positively correlated with all the non-numerical magnitudes.
evidence: This describes findings from Leibovich-Raveh et al., 2021.

claim: Archerfish proved to be able to associate different geometric shapes with different food quantities.
source: Related to magnitude discrimination, archerfish also proved to be able to associate different geometric shapes with different food quantities (Karoubi et al., 2017)
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Karoubi et al., 2017.

claim: The ability to associate geometric shapes with food quantities supports the existence of a system dealing with magnitudes in archerfish.
source: this would support the existence of a system dealing with magnitudes, although a specific role of numerical information remains unclear.
evidence: This is an interpretation of findings from Karoubi et al., 2017.

claim: The numerosities used in the study were justified by the aim to investigate how fish deal with discriminating numbers that could be supported by the ANS (large numbers, >4) and the OTS (small numbers, ≤4).
source: The numerosities used were justified by the aim to investigate how fish deal with discriminating numbers that could be supported by the ANS (large numbers, >4) and the OTS (small numbers, ≤4).
evidence: This explains the rationale for the experimental design.

claim: Previous studies showing the use of relative rules in fish employed only large numerosities.
source: Previous studies showing the use of relative rules in fish employed only large numerosities (Miletto Petrazzini et al., 2016; Miletto Petrazzini et al., 2015)
evidence: This is supported by citations to Miletto Petrazzini et al., 2016 and 2015.

claim: It remains open whether fish would use relative rules with comparisons among small numbers.
source: leaving open the question whether the same rule would be engaged even with comparisons among small numbers.
evidence: This identifies a gap in the literature that the study addresses.

claim: All different continuous physical variables such as radius, total area, total perimeter, convex-hull, and inter-distance were carefully controlled for and alternately balanced across trials.
source: All of the different continuous physical variables such as radius, total area, total perimeter, convex-hull, and inter-distance were carefully controlled for and alternately balanced across trials, ensuring that the animals could not rely on them to perform their judgement (Figure 1; see also Methods section for a detailed explanation of the randomization and experimental protocol).
evidence: This describes the methodological controls applied in the study, with reference to Figure 1.

claim: Statistical analysis confirmed that continuous physical variables were not used as a cue for numerical evaluation by archerfish.
source: Furthermore, a statistical analysis was run for a posteriori evaluation of whether any of these variables influence the archerfish responses, confirming that they were not used as a cue for numerical evaluation.
evidence: This is a conclusion from statistical analyses of the experimental data.

claim: Eight archerfish were trained to discriminate between two groups of black dots in a 3 vs 6 numerical comparison in Experiment 1.
source: Eight archerfish were trained to discriminate between two groups of black dots in a 3 vs 6 numerical comparison
evidence: This describes the sample size and training condition in Experiment 1.

claim: Four fish in Experiment 1 were trained to select the number 3.
source: four fish were trained to select the number 3, while the other four were rewarded with the number 6.
evidence: This describes the training groups in Experiment 1.

claim: Four fish in Experiment 1 were trained to select the number 6.
source: four fish were trained to select the number 3, while the other four were rewarded with the number 6.
evidence: This describes the training groups in Experiment 1.

claim: No difference was found in the number of trials needed to reach the learning criterion between the group trained with three elements (mean ± SEM = 451.25 ± 106.77) and the group trained with six elements (mean ± SEM = 413.25 ± 73.14).
source: No difference has been found in the number of trials needed to reach the learning criterion between the group trained with three elements (mean ± standard error of the mean [SEM] = 451.25 ± 106.77) and the group trained with six elements (mean ± SEM = 413.25 ± 73.14) (independent samples t-test: t(6) = 0.294, p = 0.779).
evidence: This is a statistical result from the training phase of Experiment 1.

claim: The learning criterion was reached after two consecutive sessions with at least 75% correct choices.
source: When the learning criterion was reached (at least 75% of correct choices for two consecutive sessions)
evidence: This describes the criterion used to determine when training was complete.

claim: Archerfish performance during training was not influenced by different non-numerical control conditions (overall area, overall perimeter, elements radius, elements' convex-hull, and inter-distance).
source: No significant differences were found between effects of groups, nor group interactions, suggesting to adopt the simplest model considering the choices with no contribution from any effect.
evidence: This is a conclusion from GLMM analysis of training data.

claim: The best model final estimate for training choices in Experiment 1 was 1.510 ± 0.097 (logarithmic odds ratio), corresponding to 0.82 in natural units.
source: The best model final estimate (logarithmic odds ratio) was 1.510 ± 0.097, corresponding to 0.82 in natural units (fraction of choices) as confirmed by a binomial test (probability of success: 81.9%, p < 0.001, 95% confidence intervals (CIs): 78.9–84.6).
evidence: This is a statistical result from the training phase of Experiment 1.

claim: The Cohen's g effect size for training performance in Experiment 1 was 0.32, indicating a large effect size.
source: The corresponding Cohen's g (see Methods section) was 0.32, indicating a large effect size.
evidence: This is a statistical measure of effect size from the training data.

claim: Test 1 was designed to discriminate whether fish represented numerosity as relative or absolute.
source: Test 1: This test was the main discriminator to understand whether at training fish represented numerosity as relative or absolute.
evidence: This describes the purpose of Test 1.

claim: Fish trained to select the smallest number 3 at training were presented with a novel discrimination 2 vs 3 in Test 1.
source: Fish trained to select the smallest number 3 at training (i.e. the smallest set in the 3 vs 6) were presented at test with a novel discrimination 2 vs 3
evidence: This describes the test condition for one group in Test 1.

claim: Fish trained to select the number 6 at training were tested with a 6 vs 9 condition in Test 1.
source: while fish trained to select the number 6 at training (i.e. largest set in the 3 vs 6) were tested with a 6 vs 9 condition.
evidence: This describes the test condition for the other group in Test 1.

claim: The use of 'relative' information should lead fish to choose the novel numerosity at test, while the use of 'absolute' information would reflect in the choice of the stimulus with the same number of elements as at training.
source: The use of 'relative' information (go for the smallest or largest) should lead the fish to choose the novel numerosity at test, while the use of 'absolute' information would reflect in the choice of the stimulus with the same number of elements as at training.
evidence: This describes the predicted outcomes for Test 1 based on different strategies.

claim: Test 2 aimed to clarify the role of the incorrect (unrewarded) training stimulus and its relevance for the fish.
source: Test 2: The second test aimed to clarify the role of the incorrect (i.e. unrewarded) training stimulus and its relevance for the fish.
evidence: This describes the purpose of Test 2.

claim: In Test 3, fish were presented with a comparison involving novel numerosities never experienced during training (5 vs 8).
source: Test 3: In the last test, fish behaviour was observed in a comparison involving novel numerosities never experienced during the training, that is, 5 vs 8.
evidence: This describes the test condition for Test 3.

claim: Test 3 allowed observing whether archerfish applied a relative representation or if the choice was at chance level.
source: This allowed observing whether archerfish applied a relative representation (go for the 'smallest' or 'largest') or if the choice was at the chance level, since no absolute numerical information experienced at training was present here.
evidence: This describes the purpose of Test 3.

claim: A trend for the contribution of the type of geometrical control was observed in test results, driven by a non-significant difference between the 'radius fixed' and 'overall area controlled' conditions.
source: Only a trend for the contribution of the type of geometrical control was observed, driven by a non-significant difference between the 'radius fixed' and 'overall area controlled' conditions (post hoc non-parametric tests adjusted with Tukey method: p = 0.063).
evidence: This is a statistical result from the test phase of Experiment 1.

claim: Every single geometrical control condition was statistically significant by chance level in the direction of the relative choice.
source: Within this trend, every single condition was statistically significant by chance level in the direction of the relative choice (log odds ratio estimates: 0.90 ± 0.13 for radius; 1.47 ± 0.21 for overall area; 1.03 ± 0.19 for overall perimeter)
evidence: This is a statistical result from the test phase of Experiment 1.

claim: Fish showed an overall strong significant preference for the relative numerosity in Experiment 1 tests (probability of success: 74.3%, p < 0.001, 95% CI: 70.5–77.8, Cohen's g = 0.24).
source: fish showed an overall strong significant preference for the relative numerosity (probability of success: 74.3%, p < 0.001, 95% CI: 70.5–77.8, Cohen's g = 0.24 medium effect size).
evidence: This is the main statistical result from the test phase of Experiment 1.

claim: Archerfish, when trained to select one of two simultaneously displayed groups of dots with different numerosities (3 vs 6 dots), use a relative numerical rule to perform novel numerical comparisons.
source: The result obtained in Experiment 1 showed that archerfish, when trained to select one of two simultaneously displayed groups of dots with different numerosities (i.e. 3 vs 6 dots), use a relative numerical rule to perform novel numerical comparisons.
evidence: This is a conclusion from the results of Experiment 1.

claim: The results in Experiment 1 confirm findings in other fish species such as angelfish and guppy.
source: These results confirm findings in other fish species such as angelfish (Miletto Petrazzini et al., 2016) and guppy (Miletto Petrazzini et al., 2015)
evidence: This compares the current findings to prior research, supported by citations.

claim: The results in Experiment 1 are different from those obtained in bees which showed a preference for absolute number.
source: but they are different from those obtained in bees which showed instead a preference for the absolute number (Bortot et al., 2019).
evidence: This contrasts the current findings with prior research in bees, supported by a citation.

claim: An important difference between fish and bees studies is related to the numerical comparison used: large numbers (>4 elements) for fish and small numbers (≤4 elements) with bees.
source: An important difference between fish and bees studies is related to the numerical comparison used: respectively, large numbers (>4 elements) for fish and small numbers (≤4 elements) with bees.
evidence: This identifies a methodological difference between studies that may explain different results.

claim: The difference in numerical ranges used might engage different systems, explaining the discrepancy between fish and bee results.
source: This might engage different systems (as reported in Introduction section), explaining the discrepancy.
evidence: This is a speculative explanation for the difference in results.

claim: The training discrimination in Experiment 1 involved two numbers (3 vs 6) that belong to the hypothesized 'small' and 'large' systems, respectively.
source: The training discrimination used in Experiment 1 involved two numbers (3 vs 6) that belong to the hypothesized 'small' and 'large' systems, respectively.
evidence: This describes a characteristic of the experimental design in relation to theoretical systems.

claim: The presence of a large number in the comparison in Experiment 1 may be enough to lead the archerfish to follow a relative rule.
source: In principle, the presence of a large number in the comparison in Experiment 1 may be enough to lead the archerfish to follow a relative rule.
evidence: This is a speculative explanation for the results that motivated Experiment 2.

claim: Four subjects were trained to select the largest number in a 2 vs 3 comparison (the number 3) in Experiment 2.
source: Four subjects were trained to select the largest number in a 2 vs 3 comparison (i.e. the number 3).
evidence: This describes the training condition in Experiment 2.

claim: All fish in Experiment 2 reached the learning criterion (trials to criterion ± SEM = 506.5 ± 97.8).
source: All fish reached the learning criterion, showing an ability to discriminate between the two numbers (trials to criterion ± SEM = 506.5 ± 97.8; Figure 4).
evidence: This is a result from the training phase of Experiment 2, with reference to Figure 4.

claim: The best model final estimate for training choices in Experiment 2 was 1.12 ± 0.12 (logarithmic odds ratio), corresponding to 0.75 in natural units.
source: The best model final estimate (logarithmic odds ratio) was 1.12 ± 0.12, corresponding to 0.75 in natural units (fraction of choices) as confirmed by a binomial test (probability of success: 75.5%, p < 0.001, 95% CIs: 70.8–79.8, Cohen's g = 0.25 large effect size).
evidence: This is a statistical result from the training phase of Experiment 2.

claim: The best model final estimate for test choices in Experiment 2 was 0.84 ± 0.16 (logarithmic odds ratio), corresponding to 0.70 in natural units.
source: The best model final estimate (logarithmic odds ratio) was 0.84 ± 0.16, corresponding to 0.70 in natural units, as confirmed by a binomial test (probability of success: 69.8%, p < 0.001, 95% CIs: 62.7–76.2, Cohen's g = 0.2 medium effect size).
evidence: This is a statistical result from the test phase of Experiment 2.

claim: Archerfish showed ability to discriminate between two different numerical groups of dots within the small numerical range in Experiment 2.
source: In Experiment 2, archerfish showed to be able to discriminate between two different numerical groups of dots within the small numerical range.
evidence: This is a conclusion from the training phase of Experiment 2.

claim: At test in Experiment 2, fish preferred the novel numerosity to the familiar three items in both 3 vs 4 and 3 vs 6 comparisons.
source: At test, fish preferred the novel numerosity to the familiar three items, in both 3 vs 4 and 3 vs 6 comparisons, confirming the use of a relative rather than absolute numerical rule.
evidence: This is a result from the test phase of Experiment 2.

claim: The results of Experiment 2 confirm the use of a relative rather than absolute numerical rule.
source: At test, fish preferred the novel numerosity to the familiar three items, in both 3 vs 4 and 3 vs 6 comparisons, confirming the use of a relative rather than absolute numerical rule.
evidence: This is a conclusion from the test phase of Experiment 2.

claim: The evidence from Experiment 2 does not match with findings in bees tested in the same numerical conditions.
source: This evidence does not match with findings in bees, tested in the same numerical conditions
evidence: This compares the current findings to prior research in bees.

claim: The spontaneous engagement of relative/absolute rule to extract numerical information may be guided by different ecological pressures experienced by different species in their phylogenetic history.
source: suggesting that the spontaneous engagement of relative/absolute rule to extract numerical information may be guided by different ecological pressures experienced by different species in their phylogenetic history.
evidence: This is a speculative explanation for differences between species.

claim: The spontaneous use of relative rules when only numerical cues are available suggests that among fish, it is more important to learn a general rule that is applicable to novel comparisons.
source: The spontaneous use of relative rules, when only numerical cues are available, suggests that among fish, it is more important to learn a general rule that is applicable to novel comparisons.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the findings.

claim: The relative rule strategy may be adopted because it could be less demanding as to memory load than an absolute judgement strategy.
source: It cannot be excluded that this strategy is adopted because it could be less demanding as to memory load than an absolute judgement strategy.
evidence: This is a speculative explanation for the use of relative rules.

claim: Archerfish can easily discriminate between small and large numerosity using the same rules.
source: Considering the results of Experiments 1 and 2, it is apparent that archerfish can easily discriminate between small and large numerosity using the same rules
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the combined results of both experiments.

claim: The results provide evidence in favour of a unique system underlying numerical discrimination in archerfish, as found in other fish species.
source: providing evidence in favour of a unique system underlying numerical discrimination as found in other fish species (Stancher et al., 2013; Potrich et al., 2015).
evidence: This is a conclusion supported by citations to prior research in other fish species.

claim: When some physical factors are balanced in the stimuli, others may be free to covary congruently with numerosity.
source: Given that it is empirically impossible to control for all these physical factors at once, as a consequence, when some are balanced, others may be free to covary congruently with numerosity (i.e. as the numerosity increases, the non-numerical information increases as well).
evidence: This describes a methodological constraint in the experimental design.

claim: Leibovich-Raveh et al. showed that archerfish' choice for the largest or smallest numerosity was influenced by the non-numerical variables that positively correlated with numerosity.
source: A previous study led by Leibovich-Raveh et al. in archerfish (Leibovich-Raveh et al., 2021) aimed to study whether the spontaneous choice for two numerically different groups of dots was influenced by how many physical variables were positively correlating with numerosity.
evidence: This describes findings from a prior study, supported by a citation.

claim: In the Leibovich-Raveh et al. study, stimuli with different congruity levels were created, ranging from 1 to 5.
source: By manipulating the geometry and spatial disposition of the elements, several stimuli with different congruity levels were created, ranging from 1 to 5 (i.e. from congruity level 1: only one physical variable was correlating positively with numerosity, to congruity level 5: all the five physical variables considered in the study were positively correlating with numerical information).
evidence: This describes the methodology of the Leibovich-Raveh et al. study.

claim: In the current study, the levels of congruity ranged from 1 to 3, depending on the different stimuli configurations.
source: Analyzing the characteristics of our stimuli, the levels of congruity (i.e. the number of physical factors positively correlating with numerosity) ranged from 1 to 3, depending on the different stimuli configurations (see Table 1).
evidence: This describes a characteristic of the stimuli used in the current study, with reference to Table 1.

claim: No correlation was present between the levels of congruity and the choices for the larger/smaller numerosity in both Experiments 1 and 2.
source: The results (reported in Figure 6) proved that no correlation was present between the levels of congruity and the choices for the larger/smaller numerosity, both for Experiments 1 and 2
evidence: This is a statistical result from the congruity analysis, with reference to Figure 6.

claim: Fish accuracy was not influenced by non-numerical variables, confirming that the relative rule adopted was mainly driven by the numerical cue.
source: This evidence suggests again that fish accuracy was not influenced by non-numerical variables, confirming that the relative rule adopted was mainly driven by the numerical cue.
evidence: This is a conclusion from the congruity analysis.

claim: In the Leibovich-Raveh study, fish were observed in a spontaneous choice task always rewarded, irrespective of the chosen stimulus.
source: However, in our study, archerfish were trained to select the stimuli with specific numerosity, while in the Leibovich-Raveh's study, fish were observed in a spontaneous choice task always rewarded, irrespective of the chosen stimulus.
evidence: This describes a methodological difference between the current study and the Leibovich-Raveh study.

claim: Magnitude information is particularly salient to archerfish but does not interfere when numerical rules are specifically engaged.
source: Taken together, these pieces of evidence might suggest that magnitude information matter and are particularly salient to archerfish, but they do not interfere when numerical rules are specifically engaged.
evidence: This is an interpretation that reconciles findings from the current study with prior research.

claim: Spatial frequency can be thought of as the number of repeating elements in a pattern per unit distance.
source: Spatial frequency can be thought of as the number of repeating elements in a pattern per unit distance, and it is mathematically described by the Fourier transform theory.
evidence: This is a definition based on established knowledge in signal processing.

claim: No control was applied to the spatial frequency of the stimuli.
source: No control was applied to the spatial frequency of our stimuli.
evidence: This describes a characteristic of the experimental design.

claim: Within each numerical test comparison, different spatial frequencies were found.
source: Within each numerical test comparison, different spatial frequencies were found (see Figure 7).
evidence: This is a result from the spatial frequency analysis, with reference to Figure 7.

claim: When the elements' radius was fixed between the two numerical arrays, the total power of the spatial frequency was higher in the smaller group than in the larger one.
source: In detail, when the elements' radius was fixed between the two numerical arrays, the total power of the spatial frequency was higher in the smaller group than in the larger one
evidence: This is a result from the spatial frequency analysis.

claim: When the overall perimeter was balanced, the total power of spatial frequency was higher in the more numerous group.
source: while the opposite was found in the groups in which the overall perimeter was balanced (total power higher in the more numerous group).
evidence: This is a result from the spatial frequency analysis.

claim: The trend in spatial frequency was maintained in all the numerical comparisons used, irrespective of the number of elements to be compared.
source: Interestingly, this trend was maintained in all the numerical comparisons used, irrespective of the number of elements to be compared.
evidence: This is an observation from the spatial frequency analysis.

claim: No correlations were found between performance accuracy and spatial frequency for any numerical comparison tested.
source: Results are reported in Figure 7, showing no correlations between any comparison (test 2 vs 3: r(4) = −0.17, p = 0.83; test 3 vs 4: r(4) = 0.15, p = 0.77; test 3 vs 6: r(4) = −0.35, p = 0.50; test 5 vs 8: r(4) = −0.08, p = 0.88; test 6 vs 9: r(4) = −0.42, p = 0.41).
evidence: This is a statistical result from the spatial frequency correlation analysis, with reference to Figure 7.

claim: The spatial frequency was not influencing archerfish performance in the numerical task.
source: These data strongly suggest that the spatial frequency was not influencing archerfish performance in the numerical task.
evidence: This is a conclusion from the spatial frequency analysis.

claim: When trained to select a specific group of elements between two numerical arrays, archerfish spontaneously generalize at test to novel numerical comparison according to a relative numerical rule.
source: Overall, our results showed that when trained to select a specific group of elements between two numerical arrays, archerfish spontaneously generalize at test to novel numerical comparison according to a relative numerical rule (select the largest/smallest) rather than an absolute numerical rule (select the specific number of items).
evidence: This is the main conclusion from both experiments.

claim: The findings are in agreement with previous results from other fish species and humans.
source: These findings are in agreement with previous results from other fish species and humans (Miletto Petrazzini et al., 2016; Miletto Petrazzini et al., 2015)
evidence: This compares the findings to prior research, supported by citations.

claim: The findings differ with respect to bees.
source: while differing with respect to bees (Bortot et al., 2019).
evidence: This contrasts the findings with prior research in bees, supported by a citation.

claim: Archerfish use a general relative judgement even when trained to discriminate between numerosities that belong to different systems (OTS for small numerosities ≤4 elements and ANS for large numerosities >4 elements).
source: Interestingly, archerfish use a general relative judgement even when trained to discriminate between numerosities that belong to different systems, namely 'OTS' for small numerosities (≤4 elements) and 'ANS' for large numerosities (>4 elements; for a review see Hyde, 2011).
evidence: This is an interpretation of the findings in relation to theoretical systems, with a citation to Hyde, 2011.

claim: In Experiment 1, archerfish showed to spontaneously use a general relative rule in all test conditions (2 vs 3, 6 vs 9, and 5 vs 8).
source: In Experiment 1, archerfish were trained with a 3 vs 6 contrast and then observed in test conditions with a 2 vs 3, 6 vs 9, and 5 vs 8 comparison. In all these tests, archerfish showed to spontaneously use a general relative rule.
evidence: This summarizes the findings from Experiment 1.

claim: In Experiment 2, fish followed the relative rule, selecting the largest group in the test comparisons 3 vs 4 and 3 vs 6.
source: In Experiment 2, subjects' performance was observed in a numerical discrimination involving only small numerosities (i.e. 2 vs 3) at training. Once again, at test, fish followed the relative rule, selecting the largest group in the test comparisons 3 vs 4 and 3 vs 6, thus ignoring the absolute number of elements (i.e. 3).
evidence: This summarizes the findings from Experiment 2.

claim: Previous findings in vertebrate species showed the use of relative numerosity judgements only in comparative assessments for large numerosities (>4).
source: Since previous findings in vertebrate species showed the use of relative numerosity judgements only in comparative assessments for large numerosities (>4) (Miletto Petrazzini et al., 2016; Miletto Petrazzini et al., 2015)
evidence: This describes prior research findings, supported by citations.

claim: The current study provides evidence that the same relative rule is engaged even when comparisons involve both small and large numerosities together (Experiment 1) as well as small numerosities only (Experiment 2).
source: here, we provide evidence that the same rule is engaged even when comparisons involve both small and large numerosities together (Experiment 1) as well as small numerosities only (Experiment 2).
evidence: This is a conclusion that highlights the novelty of the current findings.

claim: The condition in Experiment 2 offers a direct comparison with evidence in invertebrates tested only with small numbers.
source: Moreover, the latter condition offers us, for the first time, a direct comparison with evidence in invertebrates (tested only with small numbers) (Bortot et al., 2019).
evidence: This highlights the significance of Experiment 2 in relation to prior research, supported by a citation.

claim: The results support the hypothesis of a unique system for representing numerosities in archerfish, working both for small and large numbers, obeying the ANS.
source: Taken together, our results support the hypothesis of a unique system for representing numerosities in archerfish, working both for small and large numbers, obeying the ANS.
evidence: This is a theoretical conclusion drawn from the combined results.

claim: Evidence from other fish species supports the claim of a unique system for representing numerosities.
source: Evidence from other fish species supports this claim (Stancher et al., 2013; Potrich et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research in other fish species.

claim: Archerfish primarily relying on relative information of numerical groups may have ecological reasons, being more adaptive in a natural environment that constantly requires numerical/quantity judgement.
source: The reason for which archerfish primarily rely on the relative information of numerical groups may have ecological reasons, being more adaptive in a natural environment that constantly require numerical/quantity judgement.
evidence: This is a speculative explanation for the findings based on ecological considerations.

claim: Selecting the largest social group of companions or the largest food patch are easy rules that can be more efficient than using an absolute rule.
source: Selecting the largest social group of companions or the largest food patch are easy rules that can be more efficient than using an absolute rule.
evidence: This is a speculative explanation for the adaptive value of relative rules.

claim: The use of relative information may be less cognitively expensive (in terms of memory load) than the absolute one.
source: Moreover, the use of relative information may be less cognitively expensive (in terms of memory load) than the absolute one, since it does not require storing the information about the precise number of elements
evidence: This is a speculative explanation for the preference for relative rules.

claim: The discrimination using relative information could work on a simple relative comparison between magnitudes, guided by the ratio between the two.
source: the discrimination could work on a simple relative comparison between magnitudes, guided by the ratio between the two.
evidence: This is a speculative explanation for how relative rules might work.

claim: The engagement of relative rules requires a good level of abstraction and the creation of a general rule to be applied.
source: Nevertheless, the engagement of relative rules requires a good level of abstraction and the creation of a general rule to be applied to (Pepperberg and Brezinsky, 1991).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Pepperberg and Brezinsky, 1991.

claim: In fish, the use of an absolute rule may not be as convenient as the relative one, given that in most ecological contexts there is no specific optimal amount of food, partners or companions.
source: In fish, the use of an absolute rule may not be as convenient as the relative one, given that in most ecological contests there is no specific optimal amount of food, partners or companions.
evidence: This is a speculative explanation based on ecological considerations.

claim: For bees, the absolute rule may be more informative and useful in their ecological environment.
source: However, this seems not to be the case for species such as bees, which showed instead a spontaneous use of absolute numerical information, suggesting that this rule may be more informative and useful in their ecological environment.
evidence: This is a speculative explanation for differences between species based on ecological considerations.

claim: Spiders settle their attack based on the specific number of conspecifics at the nest in a natural predatory strategy context.
source: Similar evidence has been found in spiders, that, in a natural predatory strategy context, settle their attack based on the specific number of conspecifics at the nest (Nelson and Jackson, 2012).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Nelson and Jackson, 2012.

claim: The spontaneous use of a relative or absolute rule does not imply that animals are unable to use both.
source: Note, however, that the spontaneous use of a relative or absolute rule does not imply that animals are unable to use both.
evidence: This is a clarification about the interpretation of the findings.

claim: Vertebrates can be trained to learn a specific number of items in a set if forced to do it.
source: Vertebrates can be trained to learn a specific number of items in a set if forced to do it (Cantlon and Brannon, 2007; Miletto Petrazzini et al., 2015; Pepperberg, 1994; Smirnova et al., 2000).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to prior research.

claim: Bees can be trained to the numerical concepts of 'greater than' or 'smaller than'.
source: Similarly, bees can be trained to the numerical concepts of 'greater than' or 'smaller than' (Howard et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Howard et al., 2018.

claim: The spontaneous engagement of one of the two criteria (relative or absolute) is probably justified by a combination of natural constraints and/or less cognitive demand motivations that better fit for the individuals' fitness in their particular niches of adaptation.
source: The spontaneous engagement of one of the two criteria is therefore justified probably by a combination of natural constraints and/or less cognitive demand motivations that better fit for the individuals' fitness in their particular niches of adaptation.
evidence: This is a speculative explanation for the spontaneous use of different strategies.

claim: The study provides direct evidence of archerfish's ability to learn abstract numerical rules.
source: Note that, despite our study provides direct evidence of archerfish's ability to learn abstract numerical rules, this does not directly imply that number is spontaneously used in an ecological environment.
evidence: This is a conclusion about what the study demonstrates.

claim: The study does not directly imply that number is spontaneously used by archerfish in an ecological environment.
source: Note that, despite our study provides direct evidence of archerfish's ability to learn abstract numerical rules, this does not directly imply that number is spontaneously used in an ecological environment.
evidence: This is a limitation or clarification about the scope of the findings.

claim: Fish were guided to use numerical cues since it was the only variable systematically reinforced in the study.
source: Here, fish were guided to use numerical cues since it was the only variable systematically reinforced.
evidence: This describes a characteristic of the experimental design.

claim: In more ecological settings, continuous variables highly correlate with numerosity.
source: In more ecological settings, continuous variables highly correlate with numerosity, with a consequent difficulty to understand on which type of information archerfish spontaneously primarily rely on
evidence: This is a statement about ecological contexts based on general knowledge.

claim: It is difficult to understand which type of information archerfish spontaneously primarily rely on in ecological settings and whether this could push fish to use absolute or relative magnitudes.
source: with a consequent difficulty to understand on which type of information archerfish spontaneously primarily rely on and whether this could push fish to use absolute or relative magnitudes.
evidence: This is a limitation about generalizing the findings to natural contexts.

claim: Archerfish are capable of abstract numerical discrimination, not influenced by other continuous physical variables.
source: Lastly, with respect to the main question of our paper, the results showed that archerfish are capable of abstract numerical discrimination, not influenced by other continuous physical variables.
evidence: This is the main conclusion of the study.

claim: Archerfish were tested with numerical arrays well controlled for all the possible non-numerical variables (total area, perimeter, inter-distance, density, and convex-hull).
source: We tested archerfish with numerical arrays well controlled for all the possible non-numerical variables (e.g. total area, perimeter, inter-distance, density, and convex-hull).
evidence: This describes the methodological controls applied in the study.

claim: Previous studies in fish that attempted to control for non-numerical variables during the learning process were mainly focused on the overall elements' area, the elements' density, and convex-hull.
source: Note that previous studies in fish that have attempted to control for non-numerical variables during the learning process were mainly focused on the overall elements' area, the elements' density, and convex-hull (see e.g. Agrillo et al., 2012; Bisazza et al., 2014; DeLong et al., 2017).
evidence: This describes prior research approaches, supported by citations.

claim: In the current study, all the geometrical constraints were controlled.
source: In our study, all the geometrical constraints were controlled.
evidence: This describes a methodological strength of the current study.

claim: Non-numerical cues did not correlate with the animals' performance accuracy.
source: These non-numerical cues did not correlate with the animals' performance accuracy (as demonstrated by the statistical analyses), ensuring that the discrimination made by the animals was based on purely numerical information.
evidence: This is a conclusion from statistical analyses.

claim: For the first time in fish, the study focused on analyzing spatial frequency of the stimuli used.
source: Moreover, for the first time in fish, we focused our attention on analyzing spatial frequency of the stimuli used
evidence: This highlights a novel aspect of the current study.

claim: Spatial frequency does not influence archerfish performance.
source: showing that this variable does not influence archerfish performance.
evidence: This is a conclusion from the spatial frequency analysis.

claim: The total power of the spatial frequency has been described in the literature to positively increase with numerosity.
source: The total power of the spatial frequency has been described in the literature to positively increase with numerosity (MaBouDi et al., 2021)
evidence: This is supported by a citation to MaBouDi et al., 2021.

claim: In the current study's stimuli, the different geometrical constraints showed that the relationship between spatial frequency and numerosity could be reversed.
source: however, in our stimuli, the different geometrical constraints showed that it could be reversed as well.
evidence: This is a finding from the spatial frequency analysis.

claim: Elements' area and perimeter seem to play a crucial role in the distribution of the spatial frequencies' energy with respect to the elements disposition.
source: Moreover, elements' area and perimeter seem to play a crucial role in the distribution of the spatial frequencies' energy with respect to the elements disposition (inter-distance and sparsity).
evidence: This is an observation from the spatial frequency analysis.

claim: The amplitude component of the spatial frequency was not influencing archerfish numerical evaluation during the experiments.
source: All our analyses suggested that the amplitude component of the spatial frequency was not influencing archerfish numerical evaluation during our experiments
evidence: This is a conclusion from the spatial frequency analysis.

claim: The spatial frequency analysis provides useful information for further detailed investigations on the contribution of spatial frequency in fish cognition.
source: providing useful information for further detailed investigations on the contribution of such variable in fish cognition.
evidence: This is a statement about the implications of the findings for future research.

claim: In all studies carried out so far, the focus was on the amplitude of the spatial frequency as the main component.
source: Note, however, that in all studies carried out so far (including our own analysis), the focus was on the amplitude of the spatial frequency as the main component
evidence: This is a statement about the state of the literature.

claim: The amplitude component of spatial frequency provides information on the alternation rate of different elements in the image.
source: which provides information on the alternation rate of different elements in the image.
evidence: This is a statement about what the amplitude component represents.

claim: A more specific role on computation of numerosity is likely played by the spatial frequency phase component.
source: It is likely that a more specific role on computation of numerosity is played by the spatial frequency phase component (related to elements' spatial coherence and distribution) which directly relates to figure-ground segregation and unity formation.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about what might be important for future research.

claim: The spatial frequency phase component is related to elements' spatial coherence and distribution.
source: It is likely that a more specific role on computation of numerosity is played by the spatial frequency phase component (related to elements' spatial coherence and distribution)
evidence: This is a statement about what the phase component represents.

claim: The spatial frequency phase component directly relates to figure-ground segregation and unity formation.
source: which directly relates to figure-ground segregation and unity formation.
evidence: This is a statement about the role of the phase component based on established knowledge.

claim: Under conditions of strict control of continuous physical variables, archerfish can encode an abstract concept of number to support relative numerical judgement for both small and large numerosities.
source: In conclusion, our results provide clear evidence that under conditions of strict control of continuous physical variables, archerfish can encode an abstract concept of number to support relative numerical judgement for both small and large numerosities.
evidence: This is the final conclusion of the study.

claim: Sixteen adult archerfish (Toxotes jaculatrix) with fish size ranging between 8 and 10 cm in length were used in the study.
source: Sixteen adult archerfish, T. jaculatrix (fish size ranged between 8 and 10 cm in length) were provided by a local commercial supplier ('Acquario G di Segatta Stefano', Trento, Italy).
evidence: This describes the subjects used in the study.

claim: A group of eight fish took part in Experiment 1.
source: A group of fish (N = 8) took part in Experiment 1, while a second group (N = 4) took part in Experiment 2.
evidence: This describes the sample allocation.

claim: A group of four fish took part in Experiment 2.
source: A group of fish (N = 8) took part in Experiment 1, while a second group (N = 4) took part in Experiment 2.
evidence: This describes the sample allocation.

claim: Four animals were excluded because they did not show any consistent motivation in hitting the screen, failing to get through the different steps of the pre-training phase.
source: The other four animals were excluded because they did not show any consistent motivation in hitting the screen, failing to get through the different steps of the pre-training phase (see 'General procedure' paragraph).
evidence: This describes subject exclusion criteria and outcomes.

claim: The stimuli presented in the training phase consisted of groups of black dots confined into a black outline circle (6 cm diameter).
source: The stimuli presented in the training phase consisted of groups of black dots confined into a black outline circle (6 cm diameter).
evidence: This describes the stimuli used in the study.

claim: The dots size was ranging between 3 and 12 mm, and the visual angle was in the range 0.43° and 1.72°.
source: The dots size was ranging between 3 and 12 mm, and the visual angle was in the range 0.43° and 1.72°
evidence: This describes the stimulus properties.

claim: The visual angle range of 0.43° to 1.72° has been proven to be well perceived by archerfish.
source: which has been proven to be well perceived by archerfish (Ben-Simon et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Ben-Simon et al., 2012.

claim: All the stimuli were created using the software GeNEsIS.
source: All the stimuli were created using the software GeNEsIS (Zanon et al., 2021), a Matlab program that allows to create numerical collections of stimuli controlled for several non-numerical magnitudes.
evidence: This describes the tool used to create stimuli, supported by a citation.

claim: It is mathematically impossible to balance all the non-numerical magnitudes simultaneously in two different numerical groups.
source: Given that it is mathematically impossible to balance all the non-numerical magnitudes simultaneously in two different numerical groups (e.g. when the convex-hull of the stimuli increases, the density decreases and vice versa; similarly, when the overall area of two sets of elements with different numerousness is balanced, their overall perimeter differ, etc.)
evidence: This is a statement about a mathematical constraint in stimulus design.

claim: Different sets of stimuli were created for each numerosity, controlling for some visual physical property.
source: different sets of stimuli were created for each numerosity, controlling for some visual physical property; all the possible properties were covered across the different sets during a session
evidence: This describes the stimulus design strategy.

claim: The use of different randomized control conditions allowed not to make any of the physical variables systematically reliable and rewarded.
source: Doing so, even some physical variables were not controlled in one specific condition (e.g. when the overall area of the two sets was balanced, their overall perimeter differ; when the convex-hull of the stimuli increases, the density decreases, and vice versa), the use of different randomized control conditions allowed us not to make any of the physical variables systematically reliable and rewarded.
evidence: This explains the rationale for the stimulus design approach.

claim: Numerical information was the only reliable cue to differentiate the two stimuli across all the various trials.
source: Pictures from each set were randomly presented, making the numerical information the only reliable cue to differentiate the two stimuli across all the various trials.
evidence: This is a conclusion about the experimental design.

claim: Fish were trained with daily sessions of 48 trials.
source: Fish were trained with daily sessions of 48 trials, in which continuous physical variables were controlled and changed according to the scheme reported in Figure 1
evidence: This describes the training protocol, with reference to Figure 1.

claim: On the total of 48 randomized trials, 12 trials were for each condition 'radius fixed – inter-distance' and 'radius fixed – convex-hull'.
source: In detail, on the total of 48 randomized trials, the control conditions were organized as follows: 12 trials for each condition 'radius fixed – inter-distance' and 'radius fixed – convex-hull'
evidence: This describes the trial distribution in the training protocol.

claim: Six trials were for each condition 'area – inter-distance', 'area – convex-hull', 'perimeter – inter-distance', and 'perimeter – convex-hull'.
source: 6 trials for each condition 'area – inter-distance', 'area – convex-hull', 'perimeter – inter-distance', and 'perimeter – convex-hull'.
evidence: This describes the trial distribution in the training protocol.

claim: Half of the trials had the same individual size for each dot (radius fixed conditions).
source: In this way, half of the trials had the same individual size for each dot (radius fixed conditions), allowing us to control that the fish would not pay attention to the smaller or larger elements in size.
evidence: This describes a control feature of the experimental design.

claim: Each test condition consisted of the presentation of a couple of stimuli with a novel numerical comparison.
source: Generally, each test condition consisted of the presentation of a couple of stimuli with a novel numerical comparison, aiming to see if the target numerosity learned in the training phase was represented as a relative or an absolute numerical information.
evidence: This describes the test protocol.

claim: Each test was composed of 24 probe trials not rewarded, divided into three testing days of 8 randomized trials.
source: Each test was composed of 24 probe trials not rewarded, divided into three testing days of 8 randomized trials containing all the control conditions
evidence: This describes the test protocol.

claim: In each test session, the eight test trials were shuffled and interspersed with rewarded recall training trials (32 recall in total).
source: In each test session, the eight test trials were shuffled and interspersed with rewarded recall training trials (32 recall in total) to maintain the fish motivation high during the whole test duration.
evidence: This describes the test protocol and its rationale.

claim: The order of the tests was randomized among the fish to exclude that the performance could be influenced by their order.
source: The order of the tests was randomized among the fish to exclude that the performance could be influenced by their order.
evidence: This describes a control feature of the experimental design.

claim: At the end of each test, the fish underwent a complete daily session of retraining to further exclude potential interference among the tests.
source: At the end of each test, the fish underwent a complete daily session of retraining to further exclude potential interference among the tests.
evidence: This describes a control feature of the experimental design.
